summary_md: **Software Engineering Papers ([@ComputerPapers](https://x.com/ComputerPapers/status/2116249120302133538))** shares *Repairs for Whom?* ([arXiv 2610.38610](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38610)) by Liao and Liang, finding repair evaluators (greedy replay, stronger models) pick fixes that help them rather than the deployed agent, losing real success.

referenced_urls.title: Repairs for Whom? Evaluator-Executor Mismatch in Selecting Repairs...

media.description: Abstract of the Repairs for Whom paper.
media.ocr_text: When an LLM agent fails, repair methods choose which action to replace and what to put in its place. They often score candidate repairs with greedy replay, a stronger model, an environment oracle, or a judge that reads the failed log. We ask whether these evaluators pick repairs that help the agent that will actually execute them. Holding failed trajectories and candidate single-step repairs fixed, we label every candidate with independent rollouts of the deployed policy and measure how much deployment value each evaluator's choice loses. On failures not screened for repair value, pre-specified tests show that greedy replay loses 0.08-0.13 in expected net success gain in ALFWorld and 0.06-0.13 in net reward in WebShop, relative to selection with the deployed agent's own rollouts. At an equal rollout budget, selecting repairs for Qwen2.5-7B with Qwen2.5-14B rollouts loses 0.25 in ALFWorld and 0.07 in WebShop, twenty 14B rollouts per candidate are worth no more than two of the 7B agent's
